opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Marcus, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, let's go. I sell laptops, phones, all that at an electronics store. I use AI every day, so this is kind of my thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already the best tool there is. I use it to compare specs for customers on the spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I sell more. People come in confused about AI laptops and I'm the guy who can explain it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same job, but I'd push to be the store's AI person, run little demos for customers. Maybe start posting tech videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Hyped, kind of.

S0.say: It's already the best tool there is. He uses it to compare specs for customers.
S0.think: He sells more because he can explain AI to confused customers.
S0.do: Pushes to be the store's AI person, runs demos and maybe starts posting tech videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is boring. The tech's there, just use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer beginners, sure, but I'm not a beginner at this stuff. I know AI better than most of the managers. I'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep messing about with the tools. I'd figure out the next step when it shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chill. Not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer beginners get hired, and you're 19 in an entry job. How does that fit with being fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair. I guess I'm a beginner on paper. But I reckon knowing the tech counts for more than a CV. I hope so, anyway.

S1.say: Slow is boring. The tech's there, so use it.
S1.think: He's a beginner on paper but knows AI better than most managers, and hopes that counts for more than a CV.
S1.do: Keeps working and playing with the tools, and plans to work out the next step when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge. New jobs are coming, and the people who get AI will get them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this is my chance. All these AI jobs appearing, and I'm already using it all day. I don't know exactly what the jobs are, but I'd want one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look up what these new AI jobs actually are and maybe do a free online course. Probably. I'd also ask my manager about moving to the online sales side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Maybe a bit nervous, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'probably' about the course. What would actually stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Me, mostly. I start stuff and don't finish it. But if a real job was on the other end, I'd do it.

S2.say: This is huge. New AI jobs are coming and people who get AI will get them.
S2.think: It's his chance, though he doesn't know what the new jobs are. He admits he starts things and doesn't finish.
S2.do: Looks up what the new AI jobs are, maybe takes a free online course, and asks about moving to online sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if you're not using AI by now, that's on you. Also, the government can't just tax everything, that kills it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one's weirder. If AI's as good as professionals, what do they need me for? Customers can just ask their phone what laptop to buy. And everyone's getting rich off shares except me, because I've got nothing to put in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put a bit of every pay cheque into shares, even fifty bucks. I'd stay at my parents' place. And I'd look at jobs fixing or setting up gear, the hands-on stuff, since that's safe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. First time I've actually thought about it, honestly.

S3.say: If you're not using AI by now, that's on you. And taxing everything kills it.
S3.think: If customers can ask their phone what to buy, he's not needed. Everyone's getting rich on shares except him.
S3.do: Puts a little of each pay cheque into shares, stays with his parents and looks at hands-on jobs setting up or fixing gear.
S3.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots are cool, but yeah, this is getting real. Nobody's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That kills my backup. I was going to do hands-on setup work, and now robots do that too. I don't have a plan, and I don't have money. I'm living at home at 19, which is fine, but I can't stay forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd actually sit down and pick something. Maybe try to get into a company that installs or fixes the robots. I'd ask around online for how people got in. And I'd actually finish a course this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the wave I was going to ride just went past me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd figure it out when it shows up. Has it shown up here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. This is the one where I can't just wing it.

S4.say: Robots are cool, but this is getting real. Nobody's safe.
S4.think: Robots take his hands-on backup. He has no plan and no money, and can't live at home forever.
S4.do: Picks a direction, tries for a job installing or fixing robots, asks online how others got in and finishes a course.
S4.feel: Anxious, like the wave went past him.
